content: Participants were asked to engage in role-playing exercises to explore the fear of childbirth. They voluntarily assumed the role of a pregnant woman, interacting with the researcher and two co-researchers. The participants assisted in preparing and enacting scenarios using the necessary equipment for role-play. Observers were instructed to carefully observe the scenarios, take detailed notes, and discuss their observations at the conclusion of each scenario. In the first scenario, a participant played the role of a pregnant woman visiting a midwife’s office to decide on her mode of delivery. She experienced the events that unfolded during the consultation and discussed her concerns with the midwife. The second scenario depicted a woman undergoing a normal vaginal delivery, highlighting the benefits and complications she experienced. The process mirrored the first scenario, with participants engaging in similar discussions. In the third scenario, two co-researchers debated the merits of cesarean delivery versus natural delivery. One defended cesarean delivery, while the other supported natural delivery, presenting their arguments before a judge (the researcher). The delivery methods were personified, and the researcher acted as the judge. After these scenarios, participants shared stories about their friends’ or relatives’ experiences with both types of delivery. In a separate educational intervention, participants were divided into subgroups and attended a 90-minute session that included slide presentations, whiteboard discussions, and marker-based explanations. At the end of the session, participants’ questions were addressed. The WHO recommendations emphasized non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections. These included computerized decision aids designed for women with low literacy, which used multimedia formats (text, graphics, and voice-over narration) to present medical evidence in plain language. The decision aids also included value-clarification activities to help women prioritize their preferences, such as minimizing risks to themselves and their babies, considering costs, and envisioning their desired birth and recovery experiences. These tools helped women align their beliefs with their values and recognize potential conflicts in their priorities. Educational brochures, developed by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), provided evidence-based information on vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC) and cesarean delivery. These brochures described delivery methods, benefits, risks, and recovery processes, and were available in English and Spanish. Individualized prenatal education and support programs were also implemented. These programs involved personalized interactions with a research nurse and a resource person experienced in VBAC. Women in the written-information group received pamphlets detailing the benefits of vaginal birth over elective repeat cesarean sections. Another intervention involved computer-based decision aids delivered via laptops, often in the women’s homes. These tools provided detailed information on outcomes for planned vaginal delivery, planned cesarean section, and emergency cesarean section. Probabilities of outcomes were presented in numerical and pictorial formats. Decision analysis was conducted using decision trees, assigning utilities to outcomes based on individual values, and comparing strategies to recommend the one with the highest expected utility. Usual care, provided by obstetric and midwifery teams, was also included in the interventions. Women in the intervention groups received this standard care in addition to the specific interventions. Other studies focused on training healthcare professionals. For example, public health nurses received additional training to emphasize delivery modes during childbirth classes. Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines were implemented, often requiring mandatory second opinions before cesarean sections. Peer reviews and audits were conducted to evaluate cesarean indications, with feedback provided to healthcare professionals. Financial incentives were also introduced for practitioners meeting specific criteria. Audit and feedback systems, such as those using the Robson classification, were employed to identify contributors to high cesarean rates. Monthly audits and feedback sessions were held, and maternity staff received individual letters detailing cesarean section data. Meetings were conducted every three months to discuss changes in cesarean rates and related outcomes. Some interventions included local opinion leaders who facilitated workshops, distributed practice guidelines, and maintained educational contacts. Control groups received mailed copies of guidelines with letters encouraging implementation. These interventions aimed to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections by addressing both patient and healthcare professional factors, promoting informed decision-making, and emphasizing evidence-based practices.
